cells.source: # Notes about angular momentum and torque

The angular momentum of a point mass is defined as
$$
\vec{L}_O(t) = \vec{r}(t) \times \vec{p}(t) = m (\vec{r} \times \vec{v} ),
$$
where $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{p}= m \vec{v}$ are the position and momentum vectors.
It is important to remember that the subscript indicates that it depends on the reference point (coordinate center) that was selected to define it.
Since it is defined as a vector cross product, it means that it is perpendicular to the vectors that define it. For example, if we take a coordinate system $\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2,\hat{e}_3$ with coordinate center at $O$, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{r} = \rho \, \hat{e}_1 \\
\vec{p} = m v \, \hat{e}_2
\end{aligned},
$$
where $\rho$ is the distance in the radial direction.
Then the angular momentum results in
$$
\vec{L}_O = \rho \, \hat{e}_1 \times m v \, \hat{e}_2 = \rho m v \, (\hat{e}_1 \times \hat{e}_2) = \rho m v \, \hat{e}_3
$$
For example, in the case of motion that involves circular rotation, we can schematize the relationship between vectors as in the following figure:

math.latex: \vec{L}_O = \rho \, \hat{e}_1 \times m v \, \hat{e}_2 = \rho m v \, (\hat{e}_1 \times \hat{e}_2) = \rho m v \, \hat{e}_3

cells.source:
In the same way than when we said that if the sum of forces was zero then momentum was conserved, we can find an equivalent theorem for angular momentum based on torques.
Torque is defined as
$$
\vec{\tau}_O = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} ,
$$
again with respect to a point ("$O$") and thus results perpendicular to the force $\vec{F}$ and to the lever arm $\vec{r}$ that defines it, which is the vector that goes from position "$O$" to the point where the force is applied. From Newton's second law it then follows that
$$
\vec{\tau} = \frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} ,
$$
thus, torques define changes in angular momentum and if torques cancel out in some direction, angular momentum is conserved in that direction. The indication of the selected origin has been omitted here.
And in the same way as for the sum of forces, in the case of the sum of torques we have
$$
\vec{\tau}_{\text{total}} = \sum_i \vec{\tau}_i = \frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} .
$$
Thus the force $\vec{F}$ and the force arm $\vec{r}$ determine the torque of a system, as shown in the following figure:

It's important to remember that the force arm extends to the position where the force is applied. This is why if we want to open a door, for example, we have to apply more force if we open it by pulling close to the axis of rotation than far from it. To achieve the same torque we have to increase the force because the force arm has changed.

Furthermore, in the second part of the course we are going to look at angular momentum and torques applied to rigid bodies. From basic physics courses we know that:
$$
\vec{L} = I \vec{\omega}
$$
which we have already used in some exercises.
